questions.question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.

ANXIOUS
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Apprehensive**’.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **ANXIOUS**: The word 'Anxious' is an adjective that conveys a feeling of worry, unease, or nervousness, typically about an imminent event or something with an uncertain outcome. (चिंतित)

 
 
• **Example**: Sarah was anxious about her upcoming exam.
 
 
 
• **APPREHENSIVE**: The term 'Apprehensive' is an adjective as well and carries a similar meaning. It refers to being anxious or fearful that something bad or unpleasant will happen.(भयभीत)
 
 
• **Example**: He felt apprehensive about the consequences.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**, '**Apprehensive**' since it is the closest in meaning to 'Anxious'.

• **ACCEPT**: This verb refers to consent to receive or undertake something offered. **स्वीकार करना**

questions.question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.

My mother said, "I am meeting your father today."

options.text: My mother said that she were meeting my father that day.
My mother says that she was meeting my father today.
The mother said that she has been meeting my father that day.
My mother said that she was meeting my father that day.

questions.solution:
The correct indirect form of the given sentence is option 4) My mother said that she was meeting my father that day.

Explanation:

In indirect or reported speech, we report what someone said without using their exact words. The tense of the reported speech is usually shifted back one tense, and pronouns and time expressions are also changed accordingly.

In the given sentence, the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, which means that the tense of the reported speech should also be shifted back one tense. "I am meeting your father today" is in the present continuous tense, which should be changed to the past continuous tense ("was meeting") in reported speech.

Therefore, the correct indirect form of the sentence is "My mother said that she was meeting my father that day".

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.

If a product placement

P. we are either less likely to notice the placement

Q. our attention is fixated on what will happen next,

R. or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it

S. appears at the climax, the moment when
questions.solution:
The correct order of the parts of the sentence is: SQPR

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **S. appears at the climax, the moment when**
 
• This sentence sets the context by stating that a product placement occurs at the climax, which is the moment of highest intensity or suspense in a narrative.
 
• **Q. our attention is fixated on what will happen next,**
 
• The sentence starting with "our attention is fixated" describes the state of focus or concentration that occurs during the climax. At this point, the audience is eagerly anticipating what will happen next in the story.
 
• **P. we are either less likely to notice the placement**
 
• This statement suggests that due to the heightened focus on the narrative's unfolding events, there is a reduced likelihood of noticing the product placement. The audience's attention is primarily directed towards the storyline rather than the presence of any advertising.
 
• **R. or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it**
 
• In this final part, it is mentioned that if the audience does happen to notice the product placement during the climax, there is a higher chance of them being annoyed by it. This annoyance can stem from the distraction it poses or the perception of the advertisement interrupting the narrative flow.

The sentence is discussing the effects of product placement in a narrative, and the proper order of events is:

"If a product placement appears at the climax, the moment when our attention is fixated on what will happen next, we are either less likely to notice the placement or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it."

questions.question:

questions.solution:

Therefore, "late" is the correct option to complete the sentence.

questions.question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.

Meghna has taken all the cash.

options.text: All the cash had been taken by Meghna.
All the cash has been taken by Meghna.
All the cash had been taking by Meghna.
All the cash was taken by Meghna.

questions.solution:
The correct passive form of the given sentence is: "All the cash has been taken by Meghna." (Option 2)

**Explanation**

All the cash had been taken by Meghna. - This is a correct passive construction, but it uses the past perfect tense, which implies that the action was completed before another past action. In the given sentence, there is no such indication of a past action, so this option is not appropriate.

All the cash has been taken by Meghna. - This is the correct passive form of the given sentence. It uses the present perfect tense, which indicates that the action was completed in the past, but the result is still relevant in the present.

All the cash had been taking by Meghna. - This is incorrect as "taking" is not the correct form of the verb to use in a passive construction.

All the cash was taken by Meghna. - This is a correct passive construction, but it uses the past tense, which implies that the action was completed in the past and is not relevant in the present. The present perfect tense is a more appropriate choice in this case.

questions.solution: The correct option to fill in the blank No. 2 is "seemed" as it makes the sentence grammatically and contextually correct. ** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__** __ • **Seemed**: This is the past tense of the verb "seem," which is used to indicate an apparent state or condition, or to make something appear in a certain way. It is used when you are not certain about something. For example, in the sentence, "Perhaps it will rain later," the speaker is suggesting that it might rain later, but they aren't sure. • **Besides**: This can function as a preposition or an adverb. As a preposition, it means 'in addition to' or 'apart from'. For example, "Besides basketball, she also plays tennis," meaning she plays tennis in addition to basketball. As an adverb, it can mean 'moreover' or 'also'. For example, "I don't want to go to the party.
